question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${e}^{(x + 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4(x + 1){e}^{(x + 1)}=1$ that satisfies $y(-1)=7.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x + 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4(x + 1){e}^{(x + 1)} & =1 \\ {e}^{(x + 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1-4(x + 1){e}^{(x + 1)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-(x + 1)}-4(x + 1) \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({e}^{-(x + 1)}-4(x + 1))\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-(x + 1)}\,\text{d}x-4\int (x + 1)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-{e}^{-(x + 1)}-2{(x + 1)}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(-1)=7$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-1) & =7 \\ -{e}^{-0}-2\cdot {0}^{2}+C & =7 \\ C-1 & =7 \\ C & =8\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of ${e}^{(x + 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4(x + 1){e}^{(x + 1)}=1$ that satisfies the condition $y(-1)=7$ is

$$
y=-{e}^{-(x + 1)}-2{(x + 1)}^{2}+8.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x - 1)}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8{(x - 1)}^{3} & =5 \\ {(x - 1)}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5+8{(x - 1)}^{3} \\ \text{d}y & =(5{(x - 1)}^{-2}+8(x - 1))\,\text{d}x \\ \int \text{d}y & =\int (5{(x - 1)}^{-2}+8(x - 1))\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-5{(x - 1)}^{-1}+4{(x - 1)}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=6$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =6 \\ -5(1)^{-1}+4(1)^{2}+C & =6 \\ C-1 & =6 \\ C & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-5{(x - 1)}^{-1}+4{(x - 1)}^{2}+7 \\  & =-\frac{5}{(x - 1)}+4{(x - 1)}^{2}+7.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the specific solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-2(x + 2)-y}$ given that  $\,y(-2)=2.$

$y(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-1}} $)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 2)-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 2)}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 2)} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-2(x + 2)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-2(x + 2)}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 2)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 2)}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 2)}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(-2)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-2) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{0}+C) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ C-\frac{1}{2} & ={e}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{2{e}^{2}+1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-2(x + 2)-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(-2)=2$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{-{e}^{-2(x + 2)}+2{e}^{2}+1}{2}\right).
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the specific solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-2(x + 3)-y}$ given that  $\,y(-3)=2.$

$y(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-1}} $)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 3)-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 3)}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-2(x + 3)} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-2(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-2(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 3)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 3)}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(x + 3)}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(-3)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-3) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{0}+C) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ C-\frac{1}{2} & ={e}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{2{e}^{2}+1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-2(x + 3)-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(-3)=2$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{-{e}^{-2(x + 3)}+2{e}^{2}+1}{2}\right).
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8(x - 2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)$ that satisfies $y(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2)={\pi }^{2}.$ Assume that $0<(x - 2)<\pi .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8(x - 2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)+8(x - 2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)}+8(x - 2) \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)}+8(x - 2))\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)}\,\text{d}x+8\int (x - 2)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)}\,\text{d}x+4{(x - 2)}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the right-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2))+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)>0.$

Hence,

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2))+4{(x - 2)}^{2}+C.
$$

where $C={C}_{1}+{C}_{2}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2)={\pi }^{2}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2) & ={\pi }^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2})+4{\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}^{2}+C & ={\pi }^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1+{\pi }^{2}+C & ={\pi }^{2} \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8(x - 2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x - 2)$ that satisfies the condition $y(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2)={\pi }^{2}$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x - 2))+4{(x - 2)}^{2}.
$$
